overview: Land held in trust by the federal government for Native American tribes generally cannot be leased or crossed by a road, pipeline, power line or other right-of-way without approval from the Interior Department, which can slow projects for years. This bill extends to all federally recognized tribes the option, already available to some, of setting longer lease terms without fixed federal time limits. It also lets a tribe grant rights-of-way across its own land for any purpose without separate federal sign-off, as long as it follows tribal rules the Interior Secretary has approved. To be approved, those tribal rules must include an environmental review that identifies significant impacts, lets the public comment and requires the tribe to respond; the Secretary must decide within 180 days. The Secretary keeps the power to enforce or cancel rights-of-way, and people affected can petition the Secretary if a tribe breaks its own rules, after a hearing and a chance for the tribe to fix the problem. As of October 5, 2026, it had passed the Senate and was waiting for action in the House.
for: Supporters say the bill respects tribal self-government and removes slow federal paperwork that holds back housing, broadband, energy and business projects on tribal land.
against: Critics say the Secretary's approval of tribal rules is exempted from federal environmental and historic-preservation reviews, and the United States is not liable for losses on tribally granted rights-of-way, which could leave some impacts or disputes with less federal oversight.
